articles.title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake
articles.summary: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel.
body: ‘T he first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.

The Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”
points: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis.
But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel.

articles.title: Dolly Parton to Be Celebrated at L.A. Tribute Concert Featuring Instrumental Renditions of ‘Jolene,’ ‘9 to 5’ and ‘I Will Always Love You’
articles.summary: Just two months after Dolly Parton’s death, fans will have another opportunity to celebrate the country music legend’s extraordinary catalog. Fever’s popular Candlelight concert series is bringing a tribute to Parton to the Ritz-Carlton in Marina del Rey on Oct.
body: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

The concert comes amid an outpouring of tributes to the Grammy-winning singer, who died Aug. 25 following a brief battle with cancer. The hour-long performance will revisit her legacy through instrumental renditions of songs including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You,” the latter of which became an even bigger pop phenomenon after Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s “The Bodyguard.”

Orchid Quartet will lead the evening’s performance, with a tentative 15-song setlist that also includes “Islands in the Stream,” Parton’s chart-topping duet with Kenny Rogers; “Wildflowers,” which she recorded alongside Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris for their 1987 album “Trio”; and early-career selections such as “Dumb Blonde” and “Just Because I’m a Woman.” Other songs on the program include “Here You Come Again,” “Two Doors Down,” “My Tennessee Mountain Home” and “Light of a Clear Blue Morning.”

articles.title: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture
articles.summary: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview.
body: “Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence.

Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.

Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”

articles.title: Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes Are This Year’s Ultimate Deep-Cut Halloween Costume Duo
articles.summary: First came the laptop harness from “The Rehearsal.” Now it’s a pair of $8 headphones from “You Can See Everything.” Once again, Nathan Fielder has become an unlikely source of affordable Halloween costume inspiration, this time courtesy of his buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary.
body: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

The new costume inspiration comes courtesy of “You Can See Everything,” the A24 documentary Fielder co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, which opened in theaters Oct. 16 following a surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival.

The nearly three-hour film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes during the final 34 days before she began serving her prison sentence in 2023. Fielder and Oppenheim embed themselves in Holmes’ domestic life alongside her partner, Billy Evans, and their children, offering an unusually intimate portrait of the former Silicon Valley entrepreneur before her incarceration.

For a niche couples costume, the jailed tech founder also has an equally recognizable uniform: a black turtleneck, black trousers, a slicked-back blonde ponytail and her signature red lipstick. Add a Theranos-branded badge or a prop blood-testing device for good measure. The Steve Jobs-inspired ensemble has been a Halloween favorite since Holmes’ spectacular fall from grace, and most of the pieces are easy to find on Amazon or in your own closet.

articles.title: Maeve Communications Launches New York-Based Communications Company (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Maeve Communications, co-founded by industry veterans Laura Puig and Michelle Ciciyasvili, announced Monday the launch of its new publicity and strategic communications company.
body: The New York-based company will focus on entertainment, media and talent services offering project-based consultation and executive coaching services.

Michelle Ciciyasvili is a communications leader with 15 years of public relations experience across media, entertainment, lifestyle and fashion brands. She blends creative storytelling and strategic thinking with her knowledge of how entertainment, media and culture intersect with business.

Maeve is inspired by Hollywood legend Mae West who was an American actress, singer, comedian, screenwriter and playwright in the 1930s. The founders said West serves as a symbol of the company’s “no-nonsense approach” when providing direct, senior-level counsel on the basis of honest and targeted conversations for each client.

articles.title: Pedigree chums: why the movies are killing off fewer dogs
articles.summary: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch? Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch? There was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience.
body: It happened more times than you might expect. Mad Max 2, dog gets shot. Revenge, dog gets shot. Turner & Hooch, dog gets shot. Red, dog gets shot. Man with the Gun, dog gets shot. Badlands, dog gets shot. Dog Soldiers, you’ll never guess.
But how things change. These days – thanks to either political correctness gone mad or basic human decency or whatever – dogs are much less likely to be murdered in films.

A study by (of course) pet insurance firm Lassie has discovered that the number of dogs that die in movies dropped by a whopping 80% between 2020 and 2025. It reports that six years ago, 10 of the 100 highest-grossing films featured a dog dying either on or off screen. But by 2025, this number fell to just two.

Now, this could be down to any number of reasons. The first, and possibly most important, is that cinema finds itself in a perilous position. The future of the entire medium is at stake and every dollar counts, so why risk alienating a swathe of the audience by gratuitously offing a pup? Things are so bad that there is an entire website – Does the Dog Die? – purely to warn viewers of any enjoyment-spoiling canine fatalities.
points: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch?
Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch?
There was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience.

articles.title: Banijay CEO Marco Bassetti Urges European Producers to Fight for Better Terms of Trade With Hollywood: Studios and Streamers Should Provide ‘Rewards for Creativity’
articles.summary: Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, called for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade with the U.S.
body: “The real fight should focus on studios and streamers recognizing and providing rewards for creativity” in the form of retention of IP rights on the part of producers, Bassetti added. “Yet that is not what is happening.”

At least not in continental Europe. “But when I work for a TV network — especially in countries like England — I retain ownership of the intellectual property,” he noted. “If I sell a series, the rights eventually revert to me after three years and there’s a built-in incentive for the creator.”

“Here in Europe, we’re accustomed to a system like that,” Bassetti said. “If the streamers just treat production companies as mere service providers it’s a problem,” because you don’t provide an incentive for creators to work with you.

“The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit. There’s some movement regarding ‘windows’ (the sequence of release platforms)—but it’s only a partial shift. Ultimately, they [the studios and the streamers] still have total control,” he said.

articles.title: The reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever?
articles.summary: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtime. Name: The best reviewed film in history. Age: Not even out yet, except in the US and Canada.
body: Who’s in it? DiCaprio? De Niro? Both? It’s not that kind of film.
Did you say documentary? No thanks. But reviews of this particular documentary have been overwhelmingly favourable!

Three hours? Are you kidding? I know that seems long, but the Guardian’s critic called it “a stupefying and gloriously destabilising hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject”. And audiences have so far been undaunted by the long run time – it logged a phenomenal $15m at the box office in its opening weekend in the US and Canada.
Meh. And the film has earned an unprecedented Metacritic score of 99/100.

articles.title: Tom Cullen says he does not take playing LGBT roles lightly
articles.summary: Welsh actor Tom Cullen says he approaches queer roles "exactly the same" as he would a straight character.
body: Tom Cullen says he does not take the privilege of playing a gay character lightly.
Speaking at the screening of mystery-thriller Black Church Bay at the Iris Prize Festival, the Downton Abbey and House of the Dragon actor said representation mattered.
In the film, Cullen, from Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, plays a closeted man who finds he will go to any lengths to keep up appearances in his insular community.
It is not the first time Cullen has played a gay character, taking on his first ever role in 2011 British romantic drama Weekend.

articles.title: CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour to leave network after 43 years
articles.summary: The network's chief international anchor has covered wars including Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran.
body: CNN's chief international anchor, Christiane Amanpour, has announced she will leave the organisation next year after more than four decades.

The 68-year-old said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral".
CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere" and said the network will take time to celebrate her "before she departs next year".
Amanpour began working for CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international news desk, and went on to become one of the network's best-known correspondents, often reporting on conflicts and wars.

articles.title: European Film Producers Say Oscar Contender ‘La Bola Negra’ Shows Taking Big Risks Can Pay Off
articles.summary: “We have to take risks,” Domingo Corral, a producer of Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo's gay epic and Netflix's award season contender, told the MIA Market in Rome.
body: Italian and Spanish film and TV producers long used to exploring the political, social and cultural in their countries as storytellers have come up with a strategy to maintain creative freedom in an era of algorithms and global streamers.

“We have to take risks. If you don’t take risks, you will repeat and repeat the same. And that won’t lead you to the right place,” Corral told the MIA Market on Monday during a panel entitled Can Excellence Survive the Mainstream.

The former MovieStar exec and producer of Cannes breakouts Sirat and La Bola Negra, argued Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo’s gay epic featuring Glenn Close and Penelope Cruz was an example of a film not likely to inspire confidence among film commissioners, but has emerged to score at the box office in Spain and quite possibly at the Academy Awards.

“ La Bola Negra is a film about queer love, about civil war, all the words that a commissioner would tell you, ‘it’s going to be failure.’ Well, this was one of the best films at Cannes and it’s one of the contenders for an Oscar,” Corral argued.
